<reason>Side A won by establishing that only a binding IMO timetable solves the coordination deadlock between fuel producers and shipowners, creating the demand certainty necessary to unlock investment. Side A effectively rebutted Side B's feasibility objections by proposing phased rising shares rather than an immediate cliff-edge mandate, and neutralized the equity critique by arguing that vulnerable states already bear higher costs from unpriced climate damage while transitional rebates can be built into the rule. Side B mounted a strong challenge on enforcement and immediate food prices, but its alternative (carbon pricing) suffers from the same coordination and evasion problems while failing to guarantee the bankable demand needed for green fuel scale-up. Side B's closing was clipped, constituting a minor execution cost.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 2 (Turn 7), which directly answered the pressure questions by detailing a phased compliance mechanism with expiring availability exemptions and transitional rebates, effectively neutralizing Side B's claim that flexibility destroys bindingness while addressing the interim cost gap for import-dependent states.</best_rebuttal>
